title: Jelly's term 'legitimate' and violin players in New Orleans bands
summary: The article 'Jazz in the 20s', Jelly's remarks on legitimate violinists and why bands hired a reader like Manuel Manetta.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Fiddlers and reading violinists of New Orleans

blocks.x: Was that in the Jazz Digest or some paper?
What was it called? Jazz in the 20s was the title of it.
I think it was in Martin Williams' magazine. It may be in that same jazz panorama.

Panorama, it was in the panorama that he edited. I don't know where the original was. It's a very good article, I thought. What's always interested me was this use of the word legitimate. And I know you're a classical musician as well.

Yeah, a lot of other people. In fact, Jelly used that term too. I was talking about violin players, which Jelly didn't use hardly ever, as far as I know he did use on one of his records, Someday Sweetheart. But he evidently didn't look with too much favor on violins. He said even in New Orleans, the statement was he never heard any illegitimate. He called it the violin players. They were all legitimate, more or less straight players. That's usually the reason they would have them in a band too. Not maybe the main reason. One of the reasons they would have a violinist in there, and would even give him the leader's cap as the leader, because he was one guy that maybe had some classical training and could read music, and they could learn the new tunes from him, and he could buy the sheet music. That would be one excuse for having a violin there. I know that's one reason they would have Monetta, and he's implied that at times too, because they were always glad to hire him, because he could read good, and knew all the tunes, and could play the latest tune right out of the Ten Cent Store that they'd buy the Ten Cent sheet music. But we were mentioning about sales, saying a lot of the guys could read, but quite a few of them couldn't too. There was Kepard, I guess, probably couldn't read anything at all.
